claims.text: The starting material is an equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi powder blend with powder purity of at least 99.9% and oxygen below 0.1 wt%.
High-energy ball milling for 20–30 hours under high-purity argon is an appropriate powder-processing step for this alloy.
SPS at 1150 °C for 10 minutes under 60 MPa, with 100 °C/min heating and immediate water quenching, is an appropriate consolidation schedule.
The proposed milling and SPS route will produce relative density above 99.5%.
The processed alloy will have a nanocrystalline grain size below 500 nm.
The final phase mixture will contain more than 85% FCC, 10–15% BCC, and less than 5% HCP.
Keeping oxygen below 0.3 wt% suppresses HCP nucleation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Cooling faster than 300 °C/min kinetically retains the FCC/BCC mixture and prevents a diffusion-controlled transformation to HCP.
The 1100–1200 °C operating window lies below the liquidus and above the solid-solution solvus of CoCrFeNiTi.
A sintering strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1 maximizes densification without excessive grain growth.
High-energy milling raises dislocation density, reduces particle size, and thereby lowers the activation energy for sintering.
Rapid SPS produces near-theoretical density through diffusion bonding while minimizing grain growth.
The minor BCC phase arises from local compositional fluctuations or Ti enrichment.
High configurational entropy and rapid cooling cause the FCC matrix to remain dominant.
The processed alloy will exhibit a Vickers hardness of 450–550 HV10.
The processed alloy will have yield strength above 800 MPa.
The processed alloy will retain more than 10% compressive strain because brittle HCP and oxide precipitates are absent.
The hardness increase is attributable to grain refinement and solid-solution effects rather than HCP formation.
Oxygen above 0.5 wt% during milling causes HCP formation and embrittlement.
Hardness is to be measured by HV10 indentation using a 98.1 N load and a 15 s dwell time.

contradictions.description: The boundary predicts that deliberately raising oxygen above 0.5 wt% will cause HCP formation and embrittlement, but the falsification rule treats low hardness together with more than 10% HCP in that deliberately oxygen-contaminated sample as falsifying the hypothesis. That result would instead confirm the stated out-of-boundary failure mode.

The predicted limits are relative density above 99.5%, grain size below 500 nm, and HCP below 5%, whereas falsification requires porosity above 2%, grain size above 1 μm, or HCP above 10%. Intermediate results can violate the predictions without falsifying the hypothesis.
